sections.title: Dietary interventions
EB Table A.1.1: All diet and/or physical activity/exercise interventions versus control (standard or other care)

summary.text: Evidence base table (EB Table A.1.1) from the Cochrane review by Muktabhant et al. (2015) comparing all diet and/or physical activity/exercise interventions during pregnancy against standard or other care. Presents GRADE quality assessments, study counts, event rates, relative risks, absolute effects, and certainty ratings across overall and intervention-subgroup analyses for pre-eclampsia (RR 0.95, high certainty), caesarean section (RR 0.95, low certainty; diet and exercise counselling RR 0.87, high certainty), excessive gestational weight gain (RR 0.80, high certainty, with consistent reductions across diet, counselling, and supervised/unsupervised exercise subgroups), preterm birth (RR 0.91, low certainty), macrosomia (> 4000 g; RR 0.93, moderate certainty), low birth weight (< 2500 g; RR 0.88, very low certainty), induction of labour (RR 1.06, moderate certainty), shoulder dystocia (RR 1.02, moderate certainty), neonatal hypoglycaemia (RR 0.95, moderate certainty), and neonatal respiratory distress (RR 0.47, low certainty).

sections.title: EB Table A.1.3: Energy and protein dietary supplements versus control

summary.text: Evidence base table (EB Table A.1.3) from Ota et al. (2015) comparing balanced energy and protein dietary supplementation during pregnancy with control. Summarizes GRADE evidence showing reductions in small-for-gestational-age neonates (7 RCTs; RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69–0.90; 36 fewer per 1000; moderate certainty) and stillbirth (5 RCTs; RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39–0.94; 12 fewer per 1000; moderate certainty), alongside estimates for pre-eclampsia (RR 1.48, very low certainty), preterm birth (RR 0.96, moderate certainty), and neonatal death (RR 0.68, low certainty).

sections.title: EB Table A.2.1: Daily iron and folic acid supplements versus control (supplements without iron or no treatment/placebo)

summary.text: Evidence base table (EB Table A.2.1) from Peña-Rosas et al. (2015) comparing daily oral iron and folic acid supplementation during pregnancy against supplements without iron or placebo/no treatment. Presents GRADE ratings across maternal and perinatal outcomes, showing reduced maternal anaemia at term (RR 0.30, low certainty), higher maternal haemoglobin at or near term (MD 8.88 g/L higher, low certainty), increased high haemoglobin concentrations (> 130 g/L; RR 3.07, low certainty), reduced severe postpartum anaemia (RR 0.04, low certainty), reduced puerperal infection (RR 0.68, moderate certainty), reduced diarrhoea (RR 0.55, high certainty), reduced very preterm birth (< 34 weeks; RR 0.51, high certainty), and effects on maternal death, side-effects, antepartum/postpartum haemorrhage, transfusion, constipation, nausea, heartburn, vomiting, maternal satisfaction, placental abruption, pre-eclampsia, low birth weight (RR 0.84, low certainty), preterm birth (< 37 weeks; RR 0.93, high certainty), neonatal death, and congenital anomalies.

sections.title: EB Table A.2.2: Intermittent iron and folic acid supplements versus daily regimen with no iron

summary.text: Evidence base table (EB Table A.2.2) from Peña-Rosas et al. (2015) comparing intermittent oral iron and folic acid regimens during pregnancy against daily iron supplementation regimens. Provides GRADE evidence profiles showing higher maternal anaemia at or near term (RR 1.66, moderate certainty), lower risk of high haemoglobin concentrations (> 130 g/L) in the second or third trimester (RR 0.53, moderate certainty), fewer overall side-effects (RR 0.56, very low certainty) and nausea (RR 0.60, moderate certainty), no events of severe anaemia (< 70 g/L; moderate certainty), and low- to very-low-certainty estimates for maternal anaemia at term, severe postpartum anaemia, mean haemoglobin concentration, antepartum haemorrhage, placental abruption, diarrhoea, constipation, heartburn, vomiting, preterm rupture of membranes, low birth weight (RR 0.82), preterm birth (RR 1.03), very preterm birth, and neonatal death.
